15: # Forgejo backup retention
16: 
17: ## Overview
18: 
19: Retention decides how many Forgejo dumps are kept and for how long. In this
20: homelab the dumps land on the NAS and are pruned by age, so the policy is the
21: only thing between a full disk and a restorable history.
22: 
23: ## Details
24: 
25: - Keep 7 daily dumps and 4 weekly dumps; older ones are removed by the prune job.
26: - Retention is not controlled by `app.ini` -- the prune step is its own job.
27: - A dump is only useful if it restores, so retention never replaces a restore test.
28:

1: # AGENTS.md — 02_Knowledge
2: 
3: Structured reference notes on tech concepts, syntax guides, and foundational theory.
4: 
5: ## Why have knowledge notes?
6: 
7: - **Reference**: something to come back to when deploying or troubleshooting
8: - **Learning**: writing things down solidifies understanding
9: - **Research input**: Knowledge is the foundation that Research builds upon
10: - **Onboarding**: a single place to understand how things work
11: 
12: ## When to create
13: 
14: After an idea is promoted, or whenever you learn something worth documenting.
15: 
16: ## Status Lifecycle
17: 
18: ```
19: draft → accepted
20:   L__> archived → (move to 06_Archive/knowledge/)
21: ```
22: 
23: - **draft**: Outline or incomplete
24: - **accepted**: Reviewed and finalized
25: - **archived**: Stale or superseded
26: 
27: ## File system layout
28: 
29: ```
30: 02_Knowledge/
31: └── technologies/
32:     ├── tools/           # CLI tools, software utilities
33:     ├── services/        # specific services (forgejo, homepage, etc.)
34:     ├── kubernetes/      # k8s concepts, patterns, manifests
35:     └── hardware/        # physical hardware, specs, diagrams
36: ```
37: 
38: All names in kebab-case. Each topic is a folder with atomic notes inside. Max 3 levels deep.
39: 
40: ## Frontmatter (required)
41: 
42: ```yaml
43: ---
44: title: ""
45: status: draft        # draft | accepted | archived
46: author: ""
47: date: YYYY-MM-DD
48: tags: []
49: sources:
50:   - url: ""
51:     title: ""
52: last_audit_date: YYYY-MM-DD
53: related_docs: []
54: ---
55: ```
56: 
57: Example:
58: 
59: ```yaml
60: ---
61: title: "Ingress controllers in Kubernetes"
62: status: draft
63: author: "padawont"
64: date: 2026-08-13
65: tags: [kubernetes, networking, ingress]
66: sources:
67:   - url: "https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/ingress/"
68:     title: "Kubernetes Ingress docs"
69: last_audit_date: 2026-08-13
70: related_docs:
71:   - "./05_Implementations/node-main/traefik/overview.md"
72: ---
73: ```
74: 
75: See `./Templates/knowledge/note.md` for a copyable template.
76: 
77: ## Structure
78: 
79: ```
80: # Title
81: 
82: Overview — what is this concept? Why does it matter?
83: 
84: ## Details
85: 
86: Deep dive with examples.
87: 
88: ## Sources / Further Reading
89: ```
90: 
91: Example — abstract:
92: 
93: ```yaml
94: # simplified, vendor-neutral
95: apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
96: kind: Ingress
97: metadata: { name: example-ingress }
98: spec:
99:   rules:
100:     - host: example.com
101:       http: { paths: [{ path: /, pathType: Prefix }] }
102: ```
103: 
104: Example — real config from node-main:
105: 
106: ```yaml
107: # actual running config, may drift from this doc
108: apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
109: kind: Ingress
110: metadata: { name: forgejo-ingress, namespace: forgejo }
111: spec:
112:   ingressClassName: traefik
113:   rules:
114:     - host: git.homelab.local
115:       http: { paths: [{ path: /, pathType: Prefix }] }
116: ```
117: 
118: ## Conventions
119: 
120: - **Atomic notes**: one concept per file. When a file hits 150 lines (including frontmatter and blank lines), split it.
121: - Both abstract examples and real configs are welcome — label each block as "Example — abstract" or "Example — real config"
122: - Set `last_audit_date` on every edit; re-audit weekly
123: - Use `related_docs` to cross-link to implementations and vice-versa
124: 
125: ## Agent Behaviour
126: 
127: | Role | May | Must not |
128: |---|---|---|
129: | `worker` | read, gather sources, create and edit the note | edit files outside its brief, add unsourced claims |
130: | `reviewer` | run all five review types, emit the JSON report | edit, propose unverified fixes |
131: | `editor` | revise the note and its JSON with a cited source or rule | change anything without a citation |
132: | `spec-writer` | append a spec section referencing this note | rewrite or delete note content |
133: | `cluster-worker` | not applicable to this folder | run operational plans here |
134: 
135: Review types: `source`, `accuracy`, `scope`, `structure`, `overlap`.
136: Escalation: anything unresolved goes to the hub in the handoff `blocked:` field — never a guess.

23: # Forgejo operations — backup, restore, upgrades
24: 
25: ## Overview
26: 
27: Day-to-day operations for a self-hosted Forgejo instance: consistent backups
28: with `forgejo dump` (or snapshotting), safe upgrades between releases, and
29: restore/verification. Forgejo follows semantic versioning since 7.0.0, and the
30: database stores its schema version so a downgrade is refused automatically.
31: 
32: ## Details
33: 
34: ### Backup
35: 
36: The reliable option is a synchronized point-in-time snapshot of all storage
37: Forgejo uses. On k3s that means snapshotting the Longhorn volume
38: (`./02_Knowledge/technologies/kubernetes/longhorn/storage.md`); if storage is
39: spread across several systems (DB on one volume, repos on another), stop
40: Forgejo during the backup so the pieces stay consistent.
41: 
42: For a simple single-filesystem setup the built-in command is:
43: 
44: ```bash
45: forgejo dump
46: ```
47: 
48: - Produces a single zip containing configuration, repositories, and the
49:   database.
50: - SQLite is already included in the zip; for PostgreSQL/MySQL also take a
51:   native `pg_dump`/`mysqldump` — the SQL dump embedded by `forgejo dump` has
52:   known bugs when re-injected into a new database.
53: - Schedule it as a k8s CronJob writing to a backup location (e.g. a separate
54:   volume or object storage), keeping a few rotations.
55: 
56: ### Restore
57: 
58: 1. Stop Forgejo.
59: 2. Extract the dump zip and restore data, repos, and config to the data volume.
60: 3. Restore the native database dump (for Postgres/MySQL).
61: 4. Start Forgejo and verify:
62:    `forgejo doctor check --all --log-file /tmp/doctor.log`
63:    plus a manual web-UI walk-through (login, a repo, an issue).
64: 
65: ### Upgrades
66: 
67: Forgejo release lifecycle:
68: 
69: | Channel | Support |
70: |---|---|
71: | **Stable** (latest) | Bugfix + security fixes for ~3 months + 2-week overlap |
72: | **LTS** (version published the first quarter of every year) | Critical fixes for ~1 year 3 months |
73: | **Experimental** (dev) | Not for production |
74: 
75: Upgrade procedure:
76: 
77: 1. **Back up first** — required when moving across a stable release, wise for
78:    minor/patch.
79: 2. Read the release notes for the target version, including known problematic
80:    upgrade paths (see the upgrade guide).
81: 3. Before switching: `forgejo manager flush-queues` (queued data is not
82:    guaranteed compatible between versions).
83: 4. Perform the upgrade by replacing the container image or binary — migrations
84:    run automatically on first start.
85: 5. **Verify carefully**: `forgejo doctor check --all` plus a manual checklist.
86:    A restore after an upgrade is easy; fixing a live instance weeks later is not.

90: - Major version jumps (e.g. 15 → 16) may contain breaking changes and require
91:   the manual procedure; upgrading X → X+1 needs human verification. Staying on
92:   the `16` image tag gives minor updates automatically.
93: - Docker installs need docker >= 20.10.6.
94: - The database version guard refuses to start a downgraded binary against a
95:   newer database — do not bypass it.
96: - Subscribe to the security-announcements repo to plan security releases.

99:

101:   write logs to files via `[log]` sections (console/file modes); SQL logging
102:   is toggled by `LOG_SQL=true` in the `[database]` section.
103: - Health: rely on pod liveness/readiness probes hitting the web port; run
104:   `forgejo doctor` after any upgrade.
105: - Cross-check storage usage on the Longhorn PVC periodically.

28: ## Overview
29: 
30: Forgejo is a community-run fork of Gitea developed under the Codeberg e.V.
31: umbrella — a soft-fork in 2022 that became a hard-fork in early 2024. It is a
32: lightweight, self-hosted Git forge that provides repository hosting plus issue
33: tracking, pull requests, a package registry, and GitHub-Actions-style CI. It
34: runs as a single Go application
35: with a small resource footprint, which makes it a natural fit for a homelab
36: that wants private Git hosting without a SaaS dependency.
37: 
38: ## Details
39: 
40: ### Why self-host Git hosting
41: 
42: - **Privacy and control**: repositories, issues, and CI stay on local hardware.
43: - **No SaaS dependency**: no vendor lock-in, rate limits, or per-user cost.
44: - **Homelab-scale footprint**: a single binary plus a database (SQLite is
45:   enough for a personal instance) keeps the resource cost low.
46: 
47: ### Feature surface
48: 
49: - Repositories with protected branches, tags, and releases
50: - Issue tracking, labels, milestones, projects, and wiki
51: - Pull requests and reviews with merge-message and PR templates
52: - Package registry (container, npm, PyPI, Go, Maven, and more)
53: - Forgejo Actions — GitHub-Actions-style CI executed by `forgejo-runner`
54: - Repository mirrors (pull/push), webhooks, and an OAuth2 provider
55: - Fine-grained access tokens, 2FA, and instance moderation tools
56: 
57: ### Architecture
58: 
59: ```
60: ┌──────────┐   HTTPS   ┌──────────┐   port 3000   ┌────────────────────┐
61: │ Traefik  │ ────────► │ Forgejo  │ ────────────► │ SQLite / PostgreSQL │
62: │ (ingress)│           │ (web +   │   git over    │ / MySQL            │
63: └──────────┘           │  git)    │   SSH/HTTP    └────────────────────┘
64:                        └──────────┘       │
65:                               Longhorn PVC │  (repos + data)
66:                                            ▼
67:                                   ┌──────────────────┐
68:                                   │ forgejo-runner(s) │  ← Forgejo Actions
69:                                   └──────────────────┘
70: ```

31: # Securing a Forgejo instance
32: 
33: ## Overview
34: 
35: A homelab Forgejo instance should be locked down at three levels: transport
36: (HTTPS only via Traefik), authentication (SSH keys, 2FA, scoped tokens), and
37: instance policy (no open registration, restricted sign-in, moderation). Forgejo
38: provides fine-grained access tokens and instance settings for exactly this, and
39: its threat-analysis documentation covers the remaining risk surface.
40: 
41: ## Details
42: 
43: ### Transport
44: 
45: - Expose the instance only through HTTPS. Traefik terminates TLS on the
46:   `forgejo-ingress` (`./02_Knowledge/technologies/services/forgejo/install-config.md`).
47: - Keep `ROOT_URL` on `https://` so redirects and OAuth callbacks never downgrade.
48: - Do not port-forward raw ports 3000/22 to the public network unless the
49:   exposure is intentional.
50: 
51: ### Authentication
52: 
53: - **Local accounts**: passwords plus optional 2FA. Enforce 2FA for
54:   admins; consider it for all users.
55: - **SSH keys**: added by users under their account settings; git-over-SSH
56:   authenticates with them. The rootless container image embeds the SSH server.
57: - **Access tokens** (API/CLI): Forgejo tokens are scoped per API domain with
58:   `read:`/`write:` levels — `read:repository`, `write:issue`, `read:user`, etc.
59:   A scope is required even for public repositories. Choose the most restrictive
60:   token that works:
61:   - *All (public, private, limited)* — broadest.
62:   - *Public only* — restricted to public resources.
63:   - *Specific repositories* — limited to chosen repos and only
64:     `read/write:repository` + `read/write:issue` scopes; no admin powers.
65:   - **Least privilege**: a compromised scoped token only affects its own scope.
66: - **External auth**: OAuth2 / OpenID Connect providers can replace or supplement
67:   local logins (see the OAuth2 provider page).
68: 
69: ### Instance policy (`app.ini`)
70: 
71: | Setting | Effect |
72: |---|---|
73: | `[service] DISABLE_REGISTRATION=true` | No public sign-ups — create accounts as admin |
74: | `[service] REQUIRE_SIGNIN_VIEW=true` | Hide public views behind login |
75: | `[service] EMAIL_DOMAIN_ALLOWLIST` | Restrict sign-ups to specific domains |
76: | `[security] INSTALL_LOCK=true` | Prevent re-running the installer |
77: | `[security] SECRET_KEY` | Random instance secret set on first install |
78: 
79: ### Secrets
80: 
81: - Store `SECRET_KEY`, DB passwords, and runner tokens in a k8s Secret
82:   (`./02_Knowledge/technologies/kubernetes/concepts/secrets.md`), never in a
83:   committed manifest.
84: - Store Actions secrets scoped per repository/org rather than globally (see
85:   the CI note `./02_Knowledge/technologies/services/forgejo/ci-act-runners.md`).
86: - Rotate tokens after any suspected leak; token scope limits blast radius.
87: 
88: ### Moderation and monitoring
89: 
90: - Block users and suspend/delete accounts or repositories via the moderation
91:   tools if the instance
92:   ever opens up beyond single-owner use.
93: - Review the threat-analysis documentation for known risks (e.g. remote login
94:   propagation) before exposing the instance
95:   beyond a trusted LAN.
96: - Access control inside the cluster follows Kubernetes RBAC
97:   (`./02_Knowledge/technologies/kubernetes/concepts/rbac.md`).
98:
